newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Markets digest RBA rate cut, hungry for more.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Markets digest RBA rate cut, hungry for more.

text.p: Australian financial markets happily digested a long-anticipated cut in official interest rates on Wednesday and almost immediately began to hunger for another helping of monetary largesse.

The 0.5 point reduction in official cash rates to 6.50 percent had been discounted by markets for more than a month and was absorbed with little effort. But the money market appeared unsatisfied and began to price in another move before March.
"Certainly it's not ruling out the chance of another rate cut," said Tim Pfitzner, economist at National Australia Bank.

The futures market certainly savoured the prospect and took the March 90-bank bill contract -- which most closely reflects market thinking on where cash rates will be -- to 93.80 from 93.75 late Tuesday.
That implied a rate of 6.20 percent, suggesting investors felt another 0.50 point cut was a real possibility.

The 10-year Commonwealth bond yield had long priced in today's cut and dipped only a tick to 7.27 percent, while the Australian dollar actually bounced on relief the easing had not been larger, to touch 79 U.S. cents from an early US$0.7865. The risk of another reduction was expected to cap it there, however.
The likelihood of another cut, which would be the third since the RBA began easing on July 1, depended crucially on inflation and wages growth remaining subdued, analysts said.

"The interesting points are that the RBA in its statement talks almost exclusively about the rate reduction being linked to an improvement in inflation and wages," said Ivan Colhoun, an associate director at Bain and Co.

He thought domestic economic data over the next month would likely be weak enough to fuel talk of another cut, but cautioned the market might have to wait until the RBA board meeting in February when the bank would have Q4 inflation data at hand.

The RBA emphasised that the improvement in the inflation outlook following the sharp slowing in underlying inflation to 2.4 percent in the September quarter from 3.1 percent in Q2, had provided the scope for the economy to run faster.
Analysts did note that the central bank had not expressed any worries about the outlook for economic growth which suggested another easing was not a foregone conclusion.

"The market is starting to price in another easing, but our call at the moment is that a third cut is unlikely given there are good reasons to expect a lift in growth next year," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

In its last quarterly report on the economy, the RBA had taken an upbeat view on growth for 1997, citing strong business investment, an expected turnaround in the housing market and a still robust consumer sector.

Of these, investment was considered the most crucial both by the bank and economists, which meant the prospects for another policy easing could be made or broken by the September quarter figures on capital expenditure (CAPEX), due November 25.
"CAPEX is the next big signpost on the policy road," said Koukoulas. "If investment intentions remain as strong as they were in Q2, a rate cut will look a lot less likely."

In the June quarter, Australian investment leapt by 16.0 percent and business expectations for capital expenditure in the 1996/97 financial year were up almost 10 percent on what they had planned in the March quarter.

"The RBA may become more concerned if expectations were downgraded significantly, although even then it could take comfort in the fact that the rate cut would support investment in Q4," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at Macquarie.
"Overall, the fact the market has built in an even money chance of another half point cut by March is a fair assessment," he said. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
